question: "Rajendra I" was the son of which chola ruler?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rajaraja I.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rajendra I (also called Rajendra Chola I) was the son and successor of the great Chola ruler Rajaraja I (राजराज प्रथम).

• He ruled from about 1014 CE to 1044 CE and is regarded as one of the greatest kings of the Chola dynasty.

• Rajendra I led a victorious military expedition to the Ganga river and assumed the title 'Gangaikonda Chola', founding the new capital Gangaikonda Cholapuram.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Rajendra I extended Chola power overseas with a naval expedition against the Srivijaya Empire (Southeast Asia).

• The Chola administration was famous for its highly developed system of local self-government at the village level (Uttaramerur inscriptions).

NOTE

• Vijayalaya (Option 1): The founder of the Imperial Chola dynasty in the 9th century CE who captured Tanjore.

• Parantaka Chola I (Option 2): An early Chola ruler, remembered for the Uttaramerur inscriptions describing village administration.

• Kulothunga (Option 3): A later Chola ruler (Kulottunga I) who united the Chola and Eastern Chalukya lines.

question: As of 31st July 2025, United Nations Security Council has how many members including permanent and non-permanent members?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 15.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The United Nations Security Council (UNSC) (संयुक्त राष्ट्र सुरक्षा परिषद) has a total of 15 members.

• Of these, 5 are permanent members and 10 are non-permanent members.

• The five permanent members (P5) are the USA, UK, Russia, China and France, each holding veto power.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• The 10 non-permanent members are elected by the UN General Assembly for a two-year term.

• The UNSC is the UN organ primarily responsible for the maintenance of international peace and security.

• The headquarters of the United Nations is located in New York, USA.

NOTE

• 4 (Option 1): Not the strength of the UNSC.

• 7 (Option 2): Not related to UNSC membership.

• 11 (Option 3): Was the original size of the UNSC before it was expanded to 15 in 1965; not the current strength.

question: Who took charge as the Director General of the Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) in September 2024?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Amrit Mohan Prasad.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Amrit Mohan Prasad (अमृत मोहन प्रसाद) took charge as the Director General of the Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) in September 2024.

• The SSB (सशस्त्र सीमा बल) is a border guarding force of India deployed along the Indo-Nepal and Indo-Bhutan borders.

• It is one of the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) functioning under the Ministry of Home Affairs.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• SSB was earlier known as the Special Service Bureau, set up in 1963 after the 1962 Sino-Indian war.

• Its motto is 'Service, Security and Brotherhood'.

NOTE

• Anish Dayal Singh (Option 1): Served as the Director General of the CRPF.

• Daljit Singh Chaudhary (Option 2): Served as the Director General of the BSF (Border Security Force).

• Kuldeep Singh (Option 4): A former Director General of the CRPF.

question: Finance Minister during her budget speech 2025-26 has announced extension of Jal Jeevan Mission until ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2028.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In the Union Budget 2025-26, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced the extension of the Jal Jeevan Mission (जल जीवन मिशन) until 2028.

• The mission aims to provide Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTC) to every rural household.

• The extension came with an enhanced total outlay and a focus on quality of infrastructure and operation & maintenance.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Jal Jeevan Mission was launched in 2019 with the slogan 'Har Ghar Jal'.

• It operates under the Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation, Ministry of Jal Shakti.

NOTE

• 2035 (Option 1): Not the announced extension year for the mission.

• 2034 (Option 2): Not the correct target year.

• 2029 (Option 4): Not the year announced in the 2025-26 Budget.

question: District Project Management Units (DPMUs) initiative launched under PM Vishwakarma scheme in July 2025 comes under which ministry?
option_3: Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The District Project Management Units (DPMUs) initiative under the PM Vishwakarma scheme comes under the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (सूक्ष्म, लघु और मध्यम उद्यम मंत्रालय).

• PM Vishwakarma is a scheme to support traditional artisans and craftspeople engaged in trades such as carpentry, blacksmithy, pottery, etc.

• It provides recognition, skill upgradation, toolkit incentives, collateral-free credit and market linkage.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• PM Vishwakarma was launched on 17th September 2023 on Vishwakarma Jayanti.

• The scheme covers 18 traditional trades.

NOTE

• Ministry of Rural Development (Option 1): Handles schemes like MGNREGA and PMAY-Gramin, not PM Vishwakarma.

• Ministry of Commerce (Option 2): Deals with trade and export-import policy.

• Ministry of Agriculture (Option 4): Handles farmer welfare and agricultural schemes.

question: Which of the following sports was invented by Dr. James Naismith in 1891?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Basketball.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Basketball (बास्केटबॉल) was invented by Dr. James Naismith in 1891 in Springfield, Massachusetts, USA.

• He created the game to keep his students active indoors during winter using a soccer ball and peach baskets.

• A standard basketball team has 5 players on the court at a time.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• The international governing body of basketball is FIBA (International Basketball Federation).

• Basketball became an official Olympic sport at the 1936 Berlin Olympics.

NOTE

• Cricket (Option 2): Originated in England; governed internationally by the ICC.

• Hockey (Option 3): A team sport; India's national hockey team has a rich Olympic legacy.

• Polo (Option 4): An ancient equestrian sport with historical roots in Central Asia and Manipur (India).

question: Who among the following was part of the gold medal winning Indian hockey team of 1928 Summer Olympics?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Major Dhyan Chand.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Major Dhyan Chand (मेजर ध्यानचंद) was part of the Indian hockey team that won the gold medal at the 1928 Amsterdam Summer Olympics.

• This was India's first Olympic gold in hockey, followed by golds in 1932 and 1936.

• He is widely regarded as the greatest hockey player of all time, known as 'The Wizard'.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• India celebrates National Sports Day on 29th August, Dhyan Chand's birthday.

• The highest sporting honour of India is named the Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award.

NOTE

• Balbir Singh Sr. (Option 1): A legendary hockey player who won Olympic golds in 1948, 1952 and 1956.

• KD Jadhav (Option 3): A wrestler, India's first individual Olympic medallist (bronze, 1952).

• Sarangapani Raman (Option 4): Not associated with the 1928 gold-medal hockey team.

question: The game of judo was invented in the year ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1882.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The game of Judo (जूडो) was founded in 1882 by Jigoro Kano in Japan.

• It is a modern martial art and combat sport that developed from the older art of Jujutsu.

• The literal meaning of Judo is 'the gentle way'.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Judo became an Olympic sport at the 1964 Tokyo Olympics.

• A practitioner of judo is called a judoka, and ranks are indicated by coloured belts.

NOTE

• 1782 (Option 1): Not related to the founding of judo.

• 1812 (Option 3): Not the year judo was invented.

• 1712 (Option 4): An incorrect and much earlier date.

question: India's first Public Private Partnership Green Waste Processing plant has been set up in ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Indore.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• India's first Public Private Partnership (PPP) Green Waste Processing plant has been set up in Indore (इंदौर), Madhya Pradesh.

• Indore is consistently ranked as India's cleanest city under the Swachh Survekshan survey.

• The plant reflects Indore's leadership in waste management and sustainability initiatives.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Indore is also known for Asia's largest CNG plant from bio-CNG (Gobar-Dhan).

• Indore lies on the banks of the Khan and Saraswati rivers.

NOTE

• Patna (Option 2): The capital of Bihar, on the banks of the Ganga.

• Ranchi (Option 3): The capital of Jharkhand.

• Jamshedpur (Option 4): An industrial city in Jharkhand, home to Tata Steel.

question: 'Mando' is a slow verse and refrain composition dealing with love, tragedy and both social injustice and political resistance. It is related to which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Goa.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Mando (मांडो) is a slow, melodious verse-and-refrain musical form related to the state of Goa.

• It blends Indian and Western (Portuguese) musical traditions and deals with themes of love, tragedy, social injustice and political resistance.

• It is traditionally sung in the Konkani language.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Goa was liberated from Portuguese rule in 1961 and became a full state in 1987.

• Popular folk dances of Goa include Dekhni, Fugdi and Dhalo.

NOTE

• Uttarakhand (Option 2): Known for folk forms like Jhora and Chholiya dance.

• Bihar (Option 3): Known for folk traditions like Jat-Jatin and Bidesia.

• Tamil Nadu (Option 4): Known for classical dance Bharatanatyam and folk forms like Karagattam.

question: Who is the author of the book 'War Talk'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Arundhati Roy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The book 'War Talk' (वॉर टॉक) was written by Arundhati Roy.

• It is a collection of essays on war, nationalism, globalisation and political dissent.

• Arundhati Roy is best known for her novel 'The God of Small Things'.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• The God of Small Things won the prestigious Booker Prize in 1997.

• Her other works include 'The Ministry of Utmost Happiness' and 'Capitalism: A Ghost Story'.

NOTE

• Anita Desai (Option 2): Author of 'Fire on the Mountain' and 'Clear Light of Day'.

• Shobhaa De (Option 3): Author of 'Socialite Evenings' and 'Starry Nights'.

• Githa Hariharan (Option 4): Author of 'The Thousand Faces of Night'.

question: Who is the author of the book 'Ladies Coupe'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Anita Nair.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The book 'Ladies Coupe' (लेडीज कूप) was written by Anita Nair.

• It tells the story of a woman named Akhila and the women she meets in a ladies' railway compartment.

• Anita Nair is a well-known Indian English novelist.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Anita Nair's other works include 'The Better Man' and 'Mistress'.

• 'Ladies Coupe' has been translated into many languages worldwide.

NOTE

• Leila Seth (Option 1): First woman Chief Justice of a High Court; author of the memoir 'On Balance'.

• Twinkle Khanna (Option 3): Author of 'Mrs Funnybones' and 'The Legend of Lakshmi Prasad'.

• Nirupama Rao (Option 4): A former Foreign Secretary of India and author.

question: 'Tulip Festival' is celebrated in which of the following city?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Srinagar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Tulip Festival (ट्यूलिप महोत्सव) is celebrated in Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir.

• It is held at the Indira Gandhi Memorial Tulip Garden, Asia's largest tulip garden, on the foothills of the Zabarwan Range.

• The festival is organised in spring (March-April) to promote tourism.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• The Tulip Garden overlooks the famous Dal Lake.

• Srinagar is the summer capital of the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir.

NOTE

• Patna (Option 2): The capital of Bihar; not associated with the Tulip Festival.

• Kolkata (Option 3): The capital of West Bengal, known for the Durga Puja festival.

• Mumbai (Option 4): The financial capital of India, in Maharashtra.

question: Which district is home to the Bhitrigaon (Bhitargaon) temple, a fine example of Gupta architecture?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kanpur.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Bhitargaon temple (भितरगांव मंदिर) is located in the Kanpur district of Uttar Pradesh.

• It is a fine example of Gupta-period architecture and is one of the oldest surviving brick (terracotta) temples in India.

• It is dedicated to Lord Vishnu and dates to around the 5th century CE.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• The Gupta period is often called the 'Golden Age of India' for its achievements in art, science and literature.

• The temple is famous for its terracotta panels and a tall, curvilinear shikhara.

NOTE

• Jhansi (Option 1): A city in Uttar Pradesh known for the fort of Rani Lakshmibai.

• Gwalior (Option 3): A city in Madhya Pradesh famous for the Gwalior Fort.

• Allahabad/Prayagraj (Option 4): Known for the Triveni Sangam and Kumbh Mela.

question: 'Badhai' is a famous dance performed in which of the following state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Madhya Pradesh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Badhai (बधाई) is a famous folk dance of Madhya Pradesh, especially of the Bundelkhand region.

• It is performed on happy occasions such as festivals, births, weddings and to fulfil vows.

• It is usually associated with worship of the goddess Sheetla Mata.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Other folk dances of Madhya Pradesh include Matki, Gangaur, Grida and Maanch.

• Madhya Pradesh is known as the 'Heart of India' (Hindustan ka Dil).

NOTE

• Assam (Option 1): Known for the Bihu dance.

• Andhra Pradesh (Option 2): Known for the classical dance Kuchipudi.

• Gujarat (Option 4): Known for Garba and Dandiya Raas.

question: Which of the following is the India's first interplanetary mission?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mangalyaan.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Mangalyaan, or the Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM) (मंगलयान), was India's first interplanetary mission.

• It was launched by ISRO on 5th November 2013 and successfully entered Mars orbit on 24th September 2014.

• India became the first country to reach Mars orbit in its very first attempt.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Mangalyaan made ISRO the fourth space agency to reach Mars, after those of the USA, Russia and Europe.

• It was noted for being one of the most cost-effective Mars missions ever undertaken.

NOTE

• Shukrayaan (Option 2): A planned/future ISRO mission to study Venus.

• Chandrayaan-1 (Option 3): India's first lunar (Moon) mission, launched in 2008 — not interplanetary.

• Aditya L-1 (Option 4): India's first solar mission to study the Sun, placed at the L1 point.

question: What is the term used to describe how the brain interprets the frequency of an emitted sound?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pitch.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Pitch (तारत्व) is the term used to describe how the brain interprets the frequency of an emitted sound.

• A high-frequency sound is perceived as a high pitch, and a low-frequency sound as a low pitch.

• Pitch is a subjective (sensory) perception, while frequency is the objective physical quantity.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• The loudness of a sound depends on its amplitude.

• Frequency is measured in Hertz (Hz); humans can typically hear from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.

NOTE

• Tone (Option 1): Generally refers to the quality/character of a sound, not the brain's interpretation of frequency.

• Wavelength (Option 2): The distance between two consecutive crests or troughs of a wave.

• Frequency (Option 3): The physical number of vibrations per second, which the brain interprets as pitch.

question: Which super-fast charging battery technology was developed by Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research in 2025?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sodium-ion battery.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In 2025, scientists at the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research (JNCASR) developed a super-fast charging Sodium-ion battery (सोडियम-आयन बैटरी).

• The battery can reportedly charge up to about 80% in around 6 minutes and lasts for thousands of charge cycles.

• Sodium is far more abundant and cheaper than lithium, making it attractive for large-scale energy storage.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• JNCASR is an autonomous institution under the Department of Science and Technology (DST), located in Bengaluru.

• Sodium-ion technology is seen as a promising alternative to lithium-ion batteries.

NOTE

• Potassium-ion battery (Option 1): A different emerging battery chemistry, not the JNCASR 2025 breakthrough.

• Nion battery (Option 2): Not a recognised battery technology developed by JNCASR.

• Graphene battery (Option 4): Refers to graphene-based energy storage, not the sodium-ion work in question.

question: In which of the year was Satara annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1848.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Satara was the first state annexed by Lord Dalhousie under the Doctrine of Lapse in 1848 (विलय की नीति).

• The Doctrine of Lapse held that if a ruler died without a natural heir, his state would 'lapse' to the British and could not be inherited by an adopted heir.

• It was applied vigorously by Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General of India (1848-1856).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Other states annexed under this policy include Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854), Sambalpur and Jaipur/Udaipur.

• Resentment against the Doctrine of Lapse was one of the causes of the Revolt of 1857.

NOTE

• 1853 (Option 1): The year Jhansi was annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse, not Satara.

• 1850 (Option 2): Not the year Satara was annexed.

• 1854 (Option 3): The year Nagpur was annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse.

question: In ______, government of India set up a committee to review the fiscal reforms and suggest appropriate framework under the chairmanship of Vijay Kelkar.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2002-03.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In 2002-03, the Government of India set up a committee under the chairmanship of Vijay Kelkar (विजय केलकर) to review fiscal reforms and suggest an appropriate framework.

• The Kelkar Task Force recommended major reforms in direct and indirect taxes.

• Its recommendations aimed at simplification and rationalisation of the tax structure.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Vijay Kelkar later chaired the committee that laid the roadmap for FRBM (Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management).

• He is regarded as a key architect of India's move towards the Goods and Services Tax (GST).

NOTE

• 2000-01 (Option 1): Not the year the Kelkar committee on fiscal reforms was set up.

• 2004-05 (Option 3): Not the correct year for this committee's formation.

• 2006-07 (Option 4): An incorrect and later period.

question: As per the Industrial policy resolution 1956 of India, industries were divided into how many category?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Three.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• As per the Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR) 1956, industries were divided into three categories (तीन).

• Schedule A: Industries exclusively the responsibility of the State (17 industries).

• Schedule B: Industries progressively State-owned but with private participation allowed (12 industries); Schedule C: All remaining industries left to the private sector.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• The IPR 1956 is often called the 'Economic Constitution of India'.

• It gave the public sector a dominant/commanding role, reflecting the goal of a socialist pattern of society.

NOTE

• Two (Option 1): Not the number of categories in the 1956 resolution.

• Eight (Option 3): Incorrect; not the classification used in IPR 1956.

• Ten (Option 4): Incorrect number of categories.

question:
Which of the following is a reason of Brain drain in India?
I. Low job opportunities in India
II. Low quality of higher education in India.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Brain drain (प्रतिभा पलायन) is the emigration of highly skilled and educated people from a country in search of better opportunities.

• Statement I is correct: low job opportunities in India push talent to migrate abroad.

• Statement II is correct: perceived low quality of higher education relative to foreign institutions also encourages migration.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Other causes include higher salaries, better research facilities and a superior standard of living abroad.

• Brain drain leads to a loss of skilled human capital for the source country.

NOTE

• Only I (Option 1): Incomplete, as statement II is also a valid reason.

• Only II (Option 2): Incomplete, as statement I is also a valid reason.

• Neither I nor II (Option 4): Incorrect, since both statements are valid reasons for brain drain.

question: In the context of economy, which of the following is an example of Intermediate good?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Copper used for making utensils.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• An intermediate good (मध्यवर्ती वस्तु) is a good used as an input to produce another (final) good, not for final consumption.

• Copper used for making utensils is an intermediate good because the copper is further processed into the finished utensil.

• The value of intermediate goods is not counted separately in GDP to avoid double counting.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• A final good is one that is ready for consumption or investment and is counted in national income.

• GDP is calculated using the value of final goods and services only.

NOTE

• Shirt (Option 1): A finished item bought for final use — a final good.

• Television purchase by household (Option 3): Bought for final consumption — a final good.

• Refrigerator (Option 4): A consumer durable bought for final use — a final good.

question: Deoxygenated blood from the body enters through which of the following chamber of the heart of humans?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Right atrium.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the heart through the right atrium (दायाँ अलिंद).

• It arrives via the superior and inferior venae cavae (the largest veins).

• From the right atrium, blood passes into the right ventricle and is then pumped to the lungs for oxygenation.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• The human heart has four chambers: two atria (upper) and two ventricles (lower).

• Oxygenated blood from the lungs returns to the left atrium via the pulmonary veins.

NOTE

• Right ventricle (Option 2): Pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs, but blood does not first enter here from the body.

• Left atrium (Option 3): Receives oxygenated blood from the lungs.

• Left ventricle (Option 4): Pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body through the aorta.

question: Who among the following travelers visited India in the 7th century CE?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang).

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang) (ह्वेनसांग) was a Chinese Buddhist traveller who visited India in the 7th century CE.

• He came during the reign of Harshavardhana (Harsha) and is known as the 'Prince of Pilgrims'.

• He studied at the famous Nalanda University and wrote the account 'Si-Yu-Ki' (Records of the Western World).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Harshavardhana ruled from Kannauj in the 7th century CE.

• Xuanzang's writings are an important source for the history of Harsha's period.

NOTE

• Faxian / Fa-Hien (Option 1): A Chinese traveller who visited India in the 5th century CE during the reign of Chandragupta II.

• Megasthenes (Option 3): A Greek ambassador in the court of Chandragupta Maurya (c. 4th century BCE); wrote 'Indica'.

• Marco Polo (Option 4): A Venetian traveller who visited India in the 13th century CE.
